extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, political scientists, and practitioners interested in public opinion and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Identifying and critiquing the role of stereotypes, moral codes, and myths in shaping public opinion; detecting when stereotyped images obscure facts and how to correct for that. Useful for analysts, communicators, and civic educators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotype as economizer and blinder
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes 'economize effort' and focus energy (e.g., in wartime mobilization) but when uncritically held they 'censor out' facts that need to be taken into account and can blind people to relevant questions such as the aims or fruits of victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when a familiar image is being used to concentrate effort; deliberately ask what the ultimate aims are (e.g., 'what is victory for?') and whether the stereotype omits relevant consequences. Example: wartime focus on unlimited production without asking what victory should accomplish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for the turning point where stereotype and facts part company
rubrics_metrics.description: There is always a point when fixed images cease to fit the ebb and flow of affairs and blind spots move from the periphery into the center of attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert for signs (anticlimax, widespread disillusion) that a stereotype no longer maps reality; this requires critics willing to sound an alarm, leaders capable of understanding change, and a tolerant public to permit adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Codes and myths vs scientific hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Codes (moral, legal, professional, patriotic, etc.) rest on underlying pictures of human nature and history. Codes that are under scientific influence treat these conceptions as hypotheses; myths accept them unexamined and therefore lack the critical power to separate truth from error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the assumptions behind codes as testable hypotheses rather than unquestioned truths; demand evidence and be willing to test even the test (i.e., use the test of evidence reflexively).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral codes embed assumptions about facts and determine perception
rubrics_metrics.description: At the core of every moral code is a picture of human nature, a map of the universe, and a version of history. These assumptions shape which facts are noticed and how they are judged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating actions or public opinion, explicitly identify the factual assumptions a code presupposes (e.g., patriotic vs commercial views of human motives) and assess whether those assumptions hold in the case at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion is often a moralized and codified version of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than being a detached judgment on facts, public opinion frequently expresses a codified and moralized pattern of stereotypes that largely determines what group of facts will be seen and emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the underlying codes/stereotypes that structure a public opinion (editorial policy, ideology) rather than taking reported 'facts' as neutral; expect selective perception aligned with those codes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertness multiplies detectable aspects but can exaggerate stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Expertness increases the number of aspects we are prepared to discover and the habit of discounting expectations; however, limited expertness may also cause one to squeeze observations into existing stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value specialized knowledge but beware overfitting: experts should check whether their narrow expertise is forcing diverse phenomena into a single stereotype and seek cross-domain checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice (stereotypes) is inevitable but should be refined
rubrics_metrics.description: Because finite education requires compressed images of a complex civilization, some prejudice/stereotyping is unavoidable; the quality of thinking depends on whether these prejudices are friendly and open to refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to detect, discount, and refine prejudices rather than eliminate them; cultivate prejudices that are tolerant and oriented toward understanding rather than hatred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths lack criteria to distinguish truth from error
rubrics_metrics.description: A myth may contain important truths but, by treating its assumptions as given, it does not possess the critical mechanisms to separate its true from its false elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume longevity or utility of a belief makes it immune to scrutiny; apply evidential tests and require mechanisms for discriminating true elements from false ones within traditional beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: When factions disagree, consider differing perceptions of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents often appear perverse because they reject moral judgments or versions of facts; frequently the root is that they perceive a different set of facts shaped by different stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In dispute analysis, ask whether parties differ in the facts they attend to rather than assuming bad faith; fostering the habit of recognizing opinions as partial experiences promotes tolerance and better dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware absolutist principles that censor context and escalate conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguing from 'eternal' or absolute principles tends to censor objections, isolate issues from context, evoke strong inappropriate emotions, and can transform discussion into fighting that requires further defenses and buffers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an argument appeals to absolute principles, interrogate its applicability to concrete facts and context; prefer negotiations grounded in practical particulars over appeals to sweeping maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clue for detection: internal contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: A rapid succession or overlapping use of different absolute principles that leads to contradictions is a good clue that the argument is constructed to obliterate intervening facts rather than to seek truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for mutually inconsistent principles employed to cover different parts of an argument; contradictions indicate manufactured absolutism and signal the need to reexamine underlying facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clue for detection: failure to account for space/logistical constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereotypes can render actors incapable of taking account of practical constraints (e.g., geographic distance or logistics), projecting implausible scenarios because the stereotype excludes inconvenient facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check arguments against simple material constraints (distance, logistics, resources). If such constraints are mentally 'projected away' or ignored, the stereotype is misleading perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereotypes as rhetorical tools for persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Skilled diplomats and propagandists use a repertoire of stereotypes tailored to the expectations and sensitivities of their audiences to mobilize support for claims (territorial, political, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when rhetoric is invoking culturally resonant stereotypes rather than factual argument; assess claims by separating emotional/stereotypical appeals from empirical reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Official or canonical narratives tend to read back stereotyped qualities into events and people
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardized biographies or economic models often supply a simplified version of actors (capitalist, entrepreneur, worker) and then retroactively attribute success or failure to the qualities these models assume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating narratives of success or failure, interrogate whether the account merely projects model-based attributes onto subjects; seek alternative explanations and evidence of causal pathways rather than accepting model-consistent stories.
